title: PAUL CALLED SINGLENESS A GIFT… THEN SAID SOME PEOPLE SHOULD MARRY. WAS HE CONTRADICTING HIMSELF—OR EXPOSING SOMETHING THE CHURCH STILL GETS WRONG?
paragraphs: PAUL CALLED SINGLENESS A GIFT… THEN SAID SOME PEOPLE SHOULD MARRY. WAS HE CONTRADICTING HIMSELF—OR EXPOSING SOMETHING THE CHURCH STILL GETS WRONG?

Some Christians are ashamed because they are still single. Others are ashamed because they desperately want to be married. But hidden inside 1 Corinthians 7:7–9 is a truth that could free both groups from years of guilt, comparison, temptation, and spiritual confusion.
There is a woman somewhere tonight who loves Jesus with all her heart.
She serves at church. She prays for people. She encourages broken souls. She believes God is faithful.
But when the worship music stops, when the church lights go dark, and when she returns to an apartment where nobody is waiting for her…
The silence hurts.
She has prayed for a husband for years.
And lately, she has started wondering whether something is wrong with her.
Maybe she isn't spiritual enough.
Maybe God is withholding marriage because she has disappointed Him.
Maybe she should stop wanting companionship altogether.
After all, didn't the apostle Paul say singleness was a gift?
And somewhere else, there is a young man fighting a different battle.
He genuinely loves Christ.
He wants to honor God with his body. He wants to remain sexually pure. He wants a marriage built on Scripture rather than lust.
But his desires are real.
The temptations are real.
And every time he struggles, another voice whispers:
"If you were truly mature in Christ, you wouldn't need marriage."
So he hides.
He smiles during Bible study.
He says he is doing fine.
But privately, he wonders whether his longing for marriage is evidence that he is failing God.
Now imagine both of them opening their Bibles and reading these words:
"For I would that all men were even as I myself. But every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that." — 1 Corinthians 7:7 (KJV)
Paul appears to celebrate his own unmarried condition.
But only two verses later, he writes:
Wait.
If singleness is a gift, why would Paul encourage marriage?
If remaining unmarried can be spiritually beneficial, why would he acknowledge that some believers should marry?
And if marriage is God's beautiful design, why would Paul express a personal preference for remaining single?
The answer is not a contradiction.
It is a confrontation with something Christians have been getting wrong for centuries.
We keep trying to turn God's different gifts into a competition over who is more spiritual.
And Paul refuses to let us do it.
To understand why, we need to look beyond the English words and listen carefully to what Paul actually wrote.
In the original Greek of 1 Corinthians 7:7, Paul says:
ἕκαστος ἴδιον ἔχει χάρισμα ἐκ θεοῦ
Hekastos idion echei charisma ek Theou.
A faithful rendering is:
"Each person has his own gift from God."
Notice the word χάρισμα (charisma).
It refers to a gift graciously given.
The word belongs to the same family as χάρις (charis), meaning grace or favor.
That connection matters.
Paul is not describing a spiritual trophy awarded to the strongest Christian.
He is describing something received from God.
And notice something else.
Paul does not say everyone possesses the same gift.
He says each person has his or her own gift, one in this way and another in that.
Within this discussion, Paul recognizes differing God-given capacities and circumstances concerning singleness and marriage.
That means the believer who can faithfully serve Christ while remaining unmarried should not look down on the believer who desires marriage.
And the married believer should not treat an unmarried Christian as though that person's life is incomplete.
Different gifts do not mean different levels of worth before God.
Read that again.
Because someone has spent years believing the opposite.
Perhaps you were told that marriage is the ultimate proof of God's favor.
Perhaps people keep asking when you will finally settle down.
Perhaps every family gathering feels like an interrogation.
"Why are you still single?"
"Are you being too picky?"
"Don't you want children?"
"You're getting older, you know."
They may think they are being helpful.
But they do not hear the prayers you whisper when you are alone.
They do not see the tears.
They do not know how exhausting it can be to celebrate everyone else's wedding while wondering whether your own prayers will ever be answered.
And then someone casually says:
"Just enjoy your gift of singleness."
As though calling something a gift automatically removes every difficult emotion attached to it.
But Paul never says that a Christian who experiences loneliness must pretend loneliness does not hurt.
He never says that desiring marriage makes someone ungrateful.
And he certainly never teaches that unmarried believers are unwanted, forgotten, or spiritually defective.
In fact, the entire passage points in another direction.
Paul recognizes that people are different.
Their capacities are different.
Their circumstances are different.
And their responsibilities before God must be approached with wisdom rather than comparison.
Now we come to the part that many people misunderstand.
In 1 Corinthians 7:8–9, Paul writes:
The Greek expression translated "if they cannot contain" is:
εἰ δὲ οὐκ ἐγκρατεύονται
Ei de ouk enkrateuontai.
It means, in context, "But if they are not exercising self-control."
The verb comes from the language of self-mastery or self-control.
Paul is addressing the reality of sexual desire and the challenge of remaining continent.
He is not saying that anyone who experiences attraction is automatically incapable of singleness.
He is not teaching that sexual temptation makes marriage mandatory.
And he is not presenting marriage as permission to abandon self-control.
In fact, self-control remains a Christian virtue for both married and unmarried believers.
Marriage does not make lust holy.
Marriage does not automatically cure pornography addiction.
Marriage does not erase selfishness.
Marriage does not remove the need for repentance, discipline, tenderness, and faithfulness.
But Paul also refuses to pretend that human sexual desire does not exist.
And this is where his teaching becomes deeply compassionate.
He does not command everyone to remain single simply because he personally sees advantages in singleness.
Instead, he recognizes that marriage is an honorable and legitimate path.
That matters enormously.
Because some believers have been made to feel guilty for wanting what God Himself established as good.
Long before Paul wrote to the Corinthians, Genesis 2:18 declared:
"It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him." (KJV)
The Hebrew begins:
לֹא־טוֹב הֱיוֹת הָאָדָם לְבַדּוֹ
Lo-tov heyot ha-adam levado.
"It is not good for the human to be alone."
In its original setting, this statement introduces God's provision of a suitable counterpart for the first man and the establishment of marriage.
It does not mean that every unmarried person is living in a defective condition.
Jesus Himself lived unmarried.
Paul served Christ without a wife during the period described in this letter.
And the New Testament honors unmarried believers as full participants in God's family.
Genesis teaches us that marriage is good.
Paul teaches us that singleness can also be good.
Neither truth cancels the other.
Marriage is not a spiritual promotion. Singleness is not a spiritual punishment.
Both conditions can become places of obedience, sacrifice, holiness, and service to Jesus Christ.
But now we must face a question that may be uncomfortable.
What did Paul mean when he said it was better to marry than to burn?
The Greek phrase is:
κρεῖττον γάρ ἐστιν γαμῆσαι ἢ πυροῦσθαι
Kreitton gar estin gamēsai ē pyrousthai.
Literally:
"For it is better to marry than to burn."
In this context, the burning is commonly and appropriately understood as burning with sexual passion or desire.
Paul is not saying that unmarried Christians who struggle with desire are automatically condemned to hell.
Nor is he saying that marriage guarantees freedom from temptation.
He is making a practical pastoral judgment.
Where sustained sexual desire and difficulty exercising continence make remaining unmarried particularly challenging, marriage is a legitimate and honorable option.
And notice his wording.
"Let them marry."
Not "Let them feel ashamed."
Not "Let them pretend they have no desires."
Not "Let them prove their spirituality by enduring a lifelong condition they are not called to embrace."
Let them marry.
Paul refuses to make his personal preference a universal command.
This is especially important because he distinguishes his own judgment from a command imposed upon every believer.
In 1 Corinthians 7:6, he says:
"But I speak this by permission, and not of commandment." (KJV)
And later, in verse 35, he explains that his counsel is intended for the Corinthians' benefit, not to place a restraint upon them.
Paul is not building a prison around Christian freedom.
He is teaching believers to make faithful decisions in light of God's Word, their circumstances, and their devotion to Christ.
And the surrounding chapter gives us another important clue.
In 1 Corinthians 7:26, Paul refers to the "present distress."
The precise historical circumstances behind that expression are debated, but Paul clearly sees practical advantages to remaining unmarried amid the pressures facing his readers.
Marriage brings responsibilities.
A husband must consider his wife.
A wife must consider her husband.
Family life involves provision, sacrifice, affection, difficult decisions, and shared burdens.
None of those responsibilities is sinful.
But they are real.
Paul's concern in 1 Corinthians 7:32–35 is that believers may serve the Lord with undivided devotion.
An unmarried Christian may have opportunities for ministry, mobility, and availability that a married Christian cannot exercise in the same way.
A married Christian, meanwhile, glorifies God through covenant faithfulness, sacrificial love, and service within the household.
The question is not which person has the more impressive relationship status.
The question is:
How can I honor Christ faithfully in the life and responsibilities before me?
And perhaps this is where the passage stops being merely a theological discussion.
Because beneath the arguments about marriage and singleness, there are real people carrying real wounds.
The woman who has begun to believe she is unlovable.
The man who confuses sexual struggle with spiritual hopelessness.
The widow who misses the person she once shared everything with.
The divorced believer trying to understand Scripture while carrying regret, grief, or the consequences of someone else's betrayal.
The young Christian who is terrified of marrying the wrong person.
The single mother who wonders whether anyone will ever choose to love her and her children.
The married couple who once believed their wedding would solve everything, only to discover that two imperfect people still need the transforming grace of Jesus.
Paul's teaching does not erase these stories.
But it corrects the lie that our relationship status determines our value before God.
And here is something we must never forget.
Jesus did not die on the cross to make marriage the ultimate destination of your life.
He died and rose again to reconcile sinners to God.
Marriage is a good creation gift.
But it is not the Savior.
Singleness can be a meaningful calling or season.
But it is not the Savior either.
Jesus Christ is.
The same Jesus who spoke with the Samaritan woman in John 4 knew the complicated history of her relationships.
He knew that she had had five husbands and that the man she was then living with was not her husband.
He did not pretend her situation was irrelevant.
He spoke truthfully.
But He also offered her living water.
And that encounter changed the direction of her story.
The woman who came to the well carrying a complicated past became someone who went back to her community speaking about Jesus.
Her relationship history was not hidden from Christ.
And it did not place her beyond His reach.
That is the Gospel.
Not that our past does not matter.
Not that sin has no consequences.
Not that every desire should be fulfilled.
But that Jesus meets sinners with truth and grace, calls them to faith and repentance, and offers a new life that human relationships can never provide.
Some of us need to repent of sexual sin.
Some need to repent of treating people as objects to satisfy our loneliness.
Some need to repent of idolizing marriage.
Some need to repent of despising singleness.
Some need to repent of making married people feel superior or unmarried people feel incomplete.
And some need to stop calling themselves worthless because a prayer for marriage has not yet been answered.
You can desire marriage without worshiping marriage.
You can embrace singleness without despising marriage.
You can experience temptation without surrendering to it.
You can grieve an unmet longing without accusing God of abandoning you.
You can be married and still need healing.
You can be single and already be deeply loved by God.
But there is another truth we cannot overlook.
Marriage should never be used as an emergency escape from the hard work of becoming spiritually healthy.
If you are struggling with pornography, deception, uncontrolled anger, selfishness, or a pattern of treating people carelessly, a wedding ceremony will not magically transform those habits.
Bring those struggles into the light.
Seek accountability.
Pursue repentance.
Receive wise pastoral counsel and appropriate professional help where needed.
Learn to love others as people made in God's image, not as instruments for meeting your desires.
And if you are considering marriage, remember that Christian marriage is not merely about having a lawful outlet for sexual intimacy.
It is a covenant of faithfulness.
Ephesians 5:25 says:
"Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it." (KJV)
That is not a small calling.
A Christian husband is called to sacrificial love.
A Christian wife is not merely a solution to someone's sexual frustration.
She is a person made in God's image, worthy of honor, care, and faithful love.
And both spouses are called to live under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Paul's counsel in 1 Corinthians 7:9 should therefore never be reduced to "If you feel desire, get married quickly."
Marriage requires wisdom, mutual willingness, faithfulness, and readiness to embrace covenant responsibilities.
The presence of desire does not mean the first available relationship is God's will.
And the absence of a spouse does not mean God has forgotten your name.
Now, perhaps you are reading this while waiting for someone.
You have prayed.
You have watched friends get engaged.
You have attended weddings where you smiled for photographs and cried afterward.
You have asked God whether you will ever experience the companionship you long for.
I cannot promise you that a spouse is coming next year.
I cannot promise that your season of singleness will end.
Scripture does not authorize me to make those promises.
But I can tell you something greater.
Your life is not on hold until someone falls in love with you.
You are not half a Christian.
You are not an unfinished human being.
You are not waiting to become useful to the Kingdom of God.
You can pray now.
You can serve now.
You can grow now.
You can build friendships now.
You can pursue holiness now.
You can be part of the family of God now.
And if marriage becomes part of your story, receive it with gratitude and responsibility.
If singleness continues, do not conclude that your life has lost its purpose.
Because your deepest identity was never supposed to be "single," "married," "divorced," or "widowed."
For those who belong to Christ, the defining truth is that they are His.
Paul himself wrote in 1 Corinthians 6:20:
"For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's." (KJV)
That is the center of the Christian life.
Not finding someone who completes you.
But belonging to the One who redeemed you.
And if your past includes sexual failure, broken promises, or decisions you now deeply regret, hear the Gospel clearly.
Jesus does not invite you to hide your sin behind religious language.
He calls you to repent and believe.
He offers forgiveness through His death and resurrection.
He calls you away from the darkness and into a transformed life.
And His grace is not reserved for people whose romantic histories look impressive.
Remember what Paul told the Corinthians after naming serious sins from which believers must turn:
"And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God." — 1 Corinthians 6:11 (KJV)
"Such were some of you."
Those words carry astonishing hope.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
But in Christ, your past does not have to remain the master of your future.
There is forgiveness.
There is repentance.
There is cleansing.
There is a new direction.
There is grace that does not excuse sin but transforms sinners.
This is why the message of Gospel Warrior is so much more than a memorable phrase.
Not because Jesus guarantees every Christian a romantic happy ending.
But because He brings sinners from condemnation to forgiveness, from darkness to light, and from spiritual death to life through His saving work.
And perhaps the most unexpected thing about Paul's teaching is this:
The unmarried believer and the married believer ultimately need the same thing.
Not merely a change in circumstances.
They need Christ.
The single Christian needs Jesus more than a wedding date.
The married Christian needs Jesus more than a successful anniversary.
The lonely Christian needs the love of God and the real fellowship of His people.
The sexually tempted Christian needs grace that teaches self-control.
The wounded Christian needs truth, healing, and patient care.
And the person who has made terrible mistakes needs the Savior who still calls sinners to repentance.
So when Paul says singleness is a gift and also encourages some people to marry, he is not contradicting himself.
He is refusing to make one Christian's calling the compulsory pattern for everyone else.
He is refusing to shame legitimate marriage.
He is refusing to diminish faithful singleness.
And he is calling believers to live in wholehearted devotion to the Lord.
Maybe that is exactly what you needed to hear today.
Not another prediction about when your spouse will arrive.
Not another accusation that your desires make you spiritually weak.
Not another reminder that everyone around you seems to be moving ahead.
But a call to surrender your relationship status, your desires, your fears, your future, and your wounds to Jesus Christ.
If you are single, honor Him there.
If you are married, honor Him there.
If you are waiting, wait without surrendering your integrity.
If you are struggling, seek help without hiding behind shame.
If you have sinned, repent and run to the mercy of Christ.
If you are grieving, remember that sorrow is not proof of unbelief.
And if you are unsure what God has planned for your future, obey what He has already revealed in His Word today.
Because the goal of your life is not to prove that you are desirable enough to be chosen by another human being.
The goal is to belong faithfully to Jesus Christ, who loved His people and gave Himself for them.
And now I want to ask you something personal.
Not for a polished religious answer.
Not for something that sounds impressive.
But for something real.
Have you ever felt that being single made you less valuable, or that wanting marriage made you less spiritual?
Have you ever secretly wondered why God seems to be answering everyone else's prayers while yours remain unanswered?
"Lord, teach me to honor You in this season."
Please remember that you do not have to reveal private details to be honest with God or to receive encouragement.
And think about the people you know.
A friend who keeps questioning her worth because she is unmarried.
A young man struggling silently with temptation.
A believer recovering from heartbreak.
A married couple learning that love requires more than romantic feelings.
Someone who has drifted away from church because shame convinced them they no longer belong.
There is also something important I want to share with those who believe in this mission.
Gospel Warrior is committed to helping people encounter the truth of Scripture and grow deeper in Jesus Christ.
And we want to keep reaching more people.
More struggling believers.
More families.
More people who have questions about the Bible.
More people who have been wounded by sin, confusion, and shame.
More people who need to hear that the Gospel is not merely a message of moral improvement, but the good news of salvation through Jesus Christ.
Scripture says in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
Not through guilt.
Not through fear.
But through a shared desire to make Christ known and help others grow in biblical truth.
It is the opportunity to participate in making the Gospel known.
And whether you can give financially or not, you can still help this message reach others.
Following the page helps you stay connected to daily biblical encouragement.
Praying for this ministry is meaningful support too.
Our mission is not to build a community that depends on a personality.
It is to point people toward the Savior.
Because Gospel Warrior is not the one who saves.
Jesus Christ is.
And before you leave, remember the question that brought us here.
Why did Paul call singleness a gift but encourage some people to marry?
Because God never intended every believer to glorify Him through identical circumstances.
One person may honor Christ through faithful singleness.
Another may honor Christ through covenant marriage.
Both must resist sin.
Both must practice love.
Both must depend on grace.
Both must seek holiness.
And both must remember that no earthly relationship can replace the Lord Jesus Christ.
So tonight, whether someone is holding your hand or you are sitting alone with your Bible, do not measure God's faithfulness by the presence or absence of a wedding ring.
Look to the cross.
Look to the empty tomb.
Look to the Savior who gave Himself for sinners and rose victorious over death.
And surrender your story to Him.
Because the greatest tragedy is not reaching the end of your life without ever having been married.
It is reaching the end of your life having pursued every kind of human love while rejecting the Savior who came to reconcile you to God.
And the greatest hope is not that every lonely heart will eventually receive a spouse.
It is that everyone who repents and believes in Jesus Christ receives forgiveness and eternal life in Him.
You may still be waiting for someone to choose you—but do not miss the Savior who is calling you to follow Him today.
